source.title: Some results and open problems in research on low dimensional organic conductors

accepted.question_text: What physical mechanism explains why, in the Bechgaard salts (TMTSF)2FSO3 and (TMTSF)2ClO4, the anion-ordering temperature increases when external pressure is increased, even though the paper states that simple physical reasoning would suggest the opposite trend? The question concerns salts whose tetrahedral anions can adopt two orientations relative to the crystal lattice, and asks for a plausible microscopic explanation of the observed pressure dependence of the anion-ordering transition.

evidence.quote: Experiments on salts with anions FSO3 and ClO4 have shown that the anion ordering temperature in these two materials increases with the applied pressure [8,9], although simple physical logic would lead to contrary expectations.
To the best of the author’s knowledge no plausible physical explanation of this behaviour has been proposed.

accepted.question_text: Which effective theoretical description should be used for the electron gas in Bechgaard salts: a Luttinger-liquid description, a Fermi-liquid description, or a regime-dependent combination of the two? The paper notes that standard statistical mechanics predicts failure of the Fermi-liquid picture in strictly one-dimensional systems and favors the Luttinger-liquid model, while Bechgaard salts are physically quasi one-dimensional rather than exactly one-dimensional. The open problem is therefore to determine, with clear physical criteria, which model correctly describes these materials in which experimental situations.

evidence.quote: A very important and interesting problem in studies of Q1D organic metals is the choice of the theoretical model which can be applied to the electron gas: Luttinger or Fermi liquid?
However, the problem is open for further study, because there are numerous proofs and counter-proofs of both opinions.

accepted.question_text: How can the analytically derived conductivity of quasi-one-dimensional organic conductors in the one-dimensional Hubbard model, computed with the memory-function method, be reduced to a realistically usable form without losing the dominant physical contributions? In the paper, the exact susceptibility calculation contains about 2700 terms, so the unresolved task is to introduce realistic approximations that keep the main terms in the relevant sums while making the conductivity formula applicable to actual Bechgaard-salt physics.

evidence.quote: As an illustration, note that the sum invoked in the calculation of the susceptibility has about 2700 terms! Obviously, such a result can not be applied.
Therefore the main problem of this calculation was how to introduce realistic approximations in it, so as to make it applicable, and to take into account the main terms in various sums in it.

accepted.question_text: For Bechgaard salts modeled from the one-dimensional Hubbard Hamiltonian, what is the dependence of the electrical conductivity on band filling? Here band filling means the ratio of the number of electrons to the number of lattice sites, and experimentally it can be changed by doping with electron donors or acceptors. The open problem is to carry out the conductivity calculation and determine how conductivity varies as the filling changes, especially in relation to the thermodynamic behavior near half filling.

evidence.quote: An important characteristic of this model is the "band filling" which physically corresponds to the ratio of the number of electrons divided by the number of lattice sites.
It would be useful to perform a calculation of the conductivity, and check its behaviour as a function of the filling.

accepted.question_text: Do the phase-diagram results obtained for the one-dimensional extended Hubbard model with on-site interaction U, nearest-neighbor interaction V, and pair-hopping interaction W actually apply to organic conductors such as the Bechgaard salts? The paper reports that this continuum-limit field-theory calculation yields a rich phase diagram containing superconducting, metallic, and four insulating phases, and that the resulting diagrams resemble experimental organic-conductor phase diagrams. The unresolved question is whether that resemblance reflects genuine applicability to real organic conductors despite the omission of crystal-lattice effects.

evidence.quote: It was obtained that this model has a rich phase diagram, which contains a superconducting phase, a metallic phase and four different insulating phases.

The applicability of the results of this work to the organic conductors has not been discussed so far, but it should be noted that the phase diagrams presented in this paper bear strong resemblance to experimental results on the organic conductors.

accepted.question_text: How should one construct a theoretical conductivity model for quasi-two-dimensional organic conductors based on BEDT-TTF (ET) salts that includes as many real material parameters as possible, explicitly incorporates the crystal lattice, and can therefore be used to analyze how high external pressure affects conductivity? The paper frames this as a natural next step given the large body of conductivity measurements on Q2D salts and the expectation that doping changes the chemical potential and thereby influences transport.
accepted.context_brief: Q2D conductivity with lattice and pressure

evidence.quote: With all the avaliable experimental data on the conductivity of Q2D salts, it is tempting to undertake a theoretical study of the problem, taking into account the influence of as many as possible real material parameters.

It is particularly interesting to try to take into account in this calculation the existence of a crystal lattice, as this gives the possibility to analyze the influence of high external pressure on the conductivity.

accepted.question_text: When the electron gas in a two-dimensional lattice model for Q2D organic conductors is treated as a Fermi liquid and its chemical potential is related to measurable system parameters, what conductivity follows from applying the memory-function method, and does that conductivity calculation provide an independent argument in the debate over how the electron gas in low-dimensional systems should be modeled? This question is open because the paper states that the conductivity calculation remains future work whose conclusions are expected to bear on that modeling dispute.
accepted.context_brief: Q2D memory-function conductivity and model choice

evidence.quote: In the continuation, a calculation of the conductivity will be undertaken, using the same "memory function" method as in the case of Q1D salts.
One of the conclusions of this future work will be an independent argument in the discussions concerning modellisation of the electron gas in low dimensional systems.

accepted.question_text: What is the origin of high-temperature superconductivity? In the context of this review, the question is whether insights from low-dimensional organic conductors, fulleride-based conductors, and high-Tc materials can be integrated into a definitive explanation of the mechanism responsible for high-temperature superconductivity.

evidence.quote: In spite of world-wide efforts, the problem of the origin of high temperature superconductivity still evades a definitive solution.
